title: The Draft Line
protagonist: Aisha Rahman, route planner for a container shipping line
primary_metric: net revenue per TEU actually carried

options.A: The Canal Passage -- transit the Suez Canal on the fast route, offloading enough cargo at the load port to clear the canal's charted maximum draft
options.B: The Cape Diversion -- sail around the Cape of Good Hope with the full cargo count on board, adding the extra sailing days the longer route costs

A specific real vessel's actual voyage laden draft, draft-change-per-TEU rate, service speed, fuel consumption rate, or daily non-fuel operating cost -- all commercially private, voyage-specific or fleet-specific operational data no shipping line publishes. Became MA1-MA4 and MA7-MA8, several informed by real published reference data (S2, S5) as plausible-scale anchors.
excluded_sources: A social-media post (X/Twitter) citing Suez toll figures for large ships was found in the initial search sweep and explicitly excluded as a source -- unverifiable provenance, no way to confirm the poster's own sourcing, and social media posts are below this project's LOW-confidence floor for a load-bearing figure regardless of how plausible the numbers look.

A general-content/FAQ-style aggregator site (quartzmountain.org) giving a $10-30/TEU and $200,000-500,000 toll range was found and not used as a cited source -- no author, no stated methodology, and no primary citations of its own; Ballast Markets (S6) was preferred instead as a more clearly-dated, named-analysis alternative, though it remains MEDIUM rather than HIGH for the same underlying reason (a secondary trade-analysis piece, not a primary rate table).
scenario_constructions: Aisha Rahman and her shipping line are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention (e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case, Marcus Feld / The Manifest Split).

The M/V Coral Meridian is a disclosed scenario vessel, not a real named ship -- per the concept sheet's own explicit guidance, since any real vessel's actual voyage draft is commercial, AIS-derived data not publicly available. Its 18,000-TEU scale is chosen to be consistent with real, publicly documented ULCV classes (S2).

The vessel's laden draft (20.4 m, MA2) is deliberately constructed 0.3 m above the real, cited Suez charted limit (20.1 m, S1) to create the genuine dilemma this case is built around, representing an unusually dense cargo mix for this specific voyage -- a real, documented phenomenon (standard containerized cargo rarely fills a ULCV to its design draft; denser cargo can) rather than a claim that any real ULCV routinely exceeds the Suez limit.

The twist's expedited-alternate-carriage penalty ($1,800/TEU, FACILITATOR.md) is a disclosed scenario construction grounded in a real, general shipping-industry mechanism (missed-sailing / booked-space compensation clauses in customer service agreements), not a citation to any one real line's actual contractual rate, which is not publicly disclosed.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific vessel's voyage assignment for this scenario. Set at a scale consistent with real, publicly documented ULCV classes of this size, such as the Maersk Triple E-class (18,000 TEU nominal) [S2].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scale-setting; see sensitivity_disclosure[] -- the case's ratios are not the most fragile to this dial specifically.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Vessel laden draft at full contracted cargo count
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific vessel's actual laden draft for any one voyage. Set 0.3 m above Appendix A's real charted 20.1 m limit [S1], representing this voyage's unusually dense cargo mix.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's whole comparison is sensitive to this figure -- see sensitivity_disclosure[].

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific vessel's draft-change-per-TEU rate. Informed by real, published typical loaded-container weights (commonly cited 15-20 metric tons/TEU) and the general principle that a vessel this large changes draft by only a small fraction of a centimeter per individual TEU.

No public source publishes this specific vessel's service speed. Set within the real, commonly reported range for modern ULCVs (roughly 18-22 knots), informed by real published containership speed/fuel-consumption data for comparable vessel classes [S5].

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Suez Canal toll for this vessel
modeling_assumptions.basis: No freely-fetchable primary rate table gave an exact dollar toll for a specific vessel this session. Informed by real, dated trade-press cost analyses reporting Suez tolls in the $300,000-$800,000 range for large container ships (15,000-24,000 TEU class) [S6, MEDIUM].

A live, freely-fetchable marine-bunker price index (Ship & Bunker) could not be reached this session (HTTP 403). Informed by a real, dated trade-press benchmark reporting a 2024-2025 average VLSFO price near $600/metric ton [S6, MEDIUM].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The single most load-bearing assumption in the model -- see sensitivity_disclosure[].

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Vessel fuel consumption at service speed
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source gives this specific vessel's fuel consumption. Informed by real, published academic data for an 8,000-TEU containership (~150 t/day at 21 kn, ~225 t/day at 24 kn) [S5], scaled upward for a larger 18,000-TEU hull at a comparable 20-knot service speed.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Additional daily operating cost while at sea (beyond fuel)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific vessel's daily non-fuel operating cost (crew, insurance, schedule risk). Set at a scenario value representative of the general order of magnitude discussed in industry cost-benchmarking commentary for large containership daily opex.

sensitivity_note: No SPEC Section 6 subject-matter sensitivity applies. This is a commercial routing decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: The Canal Passage wins on tonight's actual numbers (0.96% margin) because the toll ($650,000) is small relative to the revenue difference from losing only 200 of 18,000 TEU (about 1.1% of cargo) -- the canal's much shorter transit time (22.08 days vs. 28.75) means its own fuel and operating cost, even added to the toll, is still less than what the extra 6.67 days at sea cost The Cape Diversion, letting the Canal earn slightly more per TEU actually carried.
balance.argument_b: The Cape Diversion wins if any of several real, disclosed cost or schedule assumptions move even modestly -- and a real, disclosed contractual mechanism (the twist: a per-TEU expedited-carriage penalty on the 200 containers left behind) is enough on its own to flip the verdict, because The Canal Passage's whole advantage is a thin ~$46,000 total net-revenue edge, while The Cape Diversion's full-cargo, no-penalty-risk position is structurally robust to exactly that kind of missed-sailing cost.
balance.margin_basis: Compute each route's own total voyage cost (fuel + daily operating cost for its own full transit time from D2, plus the Suez toll for The Canal Passage only), subtract from that route's revenue (TEU actually carried x freight rate per TEU), then divide by the TEU count actually carried on that route and compare the two net-revenue-per-TEU rates.
balance.model_revision_note: Revised 2026-09-18 after Tier 2 probe 1's cold solve: the original model charged The Cape Diversion's fuel/opex only for its 'extra days' over The Canal Passage (treating the shared baseline as cancelling out), which case.md's D3 wording did not unambiguously establish. A fresh cold-solve subagent read D3 the more natural way -- each route pays its own fuel/opex for its own full transit time -- and reached the same winner (A) by that route. Adopted as the case's model of record: more realistic (a ship burns fuel every day at sea regardless of route) and removes an undisclosed convention. Winner and approximate margin unchanged (was A by 0.98%, now A by 0.96%); D1/D2 figures (200 TEU offload, 22.08/28.75/6.67 days) are unaffected. case.md's D3 deliverable text was rewritten to state the convention explicitly.
balance.twist_effect: A disclosed scenario twist: the shipping line's standard customer service agreement imposes a $1,800/TEU expedited-alternate-carriage penalty on any contracted cargo that misses its booked sailing -- applied to the 200 TEU offloaded under The Canal Passage. This adds $360,000 to The Canal Passage's costs, dropping its rate to $1,576.37/TEU, below The Cape Diversion's unchanged $1,581.40/TEU -- the winner flips to B, margin 0.32%. Disclosed here and in sensitivity_model.py; never in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's student-facing sections.
balance.stability: Base margin (0.96%) is extremely thin by construction -- both options are genuinely close, per SPEC Section 2's own gold-standard precedent (the Robotics Engineering exemplar's 0.09% margin). A direct, computable function of all eight stated Modeling Assumptions via sensitivity_model.py: 5 of the 8 (draft_m, speed_kn, toll_usd, fuel_price_per_ton, fuel_tons_per_day) flip the winner at a +/-50% flex; none breach the SPEC Section 2 20% cap in either direction. This is a real, disclosed finding about how tightly this case's margin depends on undisclosed real-world operational and commercial data (voyage-specific draft, toll, and bunker price), not a defect -- see sensitivity_disclosure[].

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1 has no citable per-voyage source; it is a scale-setting scenario assumption informed by real ULCV classes (S2). Flexing +50% narrows the margin to 0.64% without flipping; -50% widens it to 1.89%, also without flipping. Not among the two most load-bearing dials.

MA2 has no citable per-voyage source. Flexing +50% flips the winner to B (8.11% margin, still under the cap); flexing -50% keeps A winning (1.11% margin). This directly changes the TEU offload count, which is the case's central lever.
MA3 has no citable per-vessel source. Flexing +50% (winner A, 1.01%) or -50% (winner A, 0.81%) does not flip the winner -- the least load-bearing of the eight dials.

MA4, informed only by real published typical ULCV speed ranges (S5's context), not a direct citation. Flexing +50% flips the winner to B (0.12% margin, essentially a dead heat); flexing -50% keeps A winning by a wider 4.96% margin.
MA5, informed only by a MEDIUM secondary trade-press range (S6), not a primary rate table. Flexing +50% flips the winner to B (0.20% margin); flexing -50% keeps A winning (2.12% margin).

MA6, informed only by a MEDIUM secondary benchmark (S6). The single most load-bearing assumption by basis strength (no primary source at all was reachable). Flexing +50% keeps A winning (2.46% margin); flexing -50% flips the winner to B (0.37% margin).

MA7, informed by real academic data (S5) for a smaller vessel class, scaled up (not a direct citation for this vessel). Flexing +50% keeps A winning (2.46% margin); flexing -50% flips the winner to B (0.37% margin) -- mirrors fuel_price_per_ton exactly, since both dials enter the model as a simple product.
MA8 has no citable per-vessel source. Flexing +50% (winner A, 1.26%) or -50% (winner A, 0.67%) does not flip the winner.

deliverables.text: A draft-and-offload calculation for The Canal Passage: find how much draft the vessel must shed to clear the canal's charted limit, and how many TEU must come off at the load port to achieve it.
A route transit-time comparison: total transit time in days for each route, and the schedule difference between them.
A net-revenue-per-TEU comparison for each route and the percent margin between them.
A one-paragraph written recommendation naming the chosen route and addressing the draft-at-limit edge case.

P7_waiver.reason: Two genuine remediation rounds were run against real, fresh cold-read subagents (2026-09-18). Round 1 added the STORY_GLOSSARY layer from scratch (0 to 9 real-linked .sterm terms: container shipping, laden/draft, stowage plan, TEU, Suez Canal, berth window, Cape of Good Hope, bunker fuel, FEU) plus a buoyancy/displacement explanation, an operating-cost breakdown clarification, and a missed-sailing-clause explanation. The cold-read count dropped from 10 named concepts to 10 (a wash on count, but qualitatively different/harder-to-fix concepts remained: beam, VLSFO, great-circle, dredged cross-sectional area, draft measurement/certification process). Round 2 added beam (sterm), spelled out VLSFO inline, explained great-circle distance, simplified the dredged-cross-section jargon, added berth-window cascading-schedule reasoning, added FEU-vs-TEU historical reasoning, and explicitly acknowledged the draft-to-offload rate as a stated simplification (naming what it deliberately does not model). The third cold-read still named 11 concepts and a Q2 (MCS-51) finding about the draft-to-offload mechanism's physical picturability. This domain (naval architecture / maritime operations) carries genuinely dense technical vocabulary -- buoyancy/displacement physics, draft certification, dredged channel geometry, and containerized-cargo handling are not reducible to a glossary entry each without turning the case into a naval-engineering primer, which would work against the case's own T3 pedagogy (SPEC SS3: some data and complexity is deliberately present for the student to navigate, not eliminate). Real, substantive effort was made across two full rounds; the remaining gap is disclosed rather than hidden or falsely marked PASS.
remaining_gaps: Draft (of a ship) -- even with the definition given, hard to picture what this looks like on an actual ship or how it is measured.
Displacement / how a floating object pushes aside water -- the case asserts the buoyancy relationship without a mental model of why it is true.
Beam (ship's width at widest point) -- defined, but why it matters for the draft limit is not fully explained.
Stowage plan -- described conceptually, but the actual document/software is not picturable.
TEU / FEU conversion logic -- the arithmetic is followed but the historical reason for two units is not fully intuitive.
Bunker fuel -- defined as heavy fuel oil, but its physical properties/handling are not described.
Charted maximum permitted transit draft / how a canal authority actually clears a vessel -- the clearance process itself is not pictured.
Berth window and schedule cascading -- understood abstractly as a time slot, not concretely how a missed window cascades through a port schedule.
Great-circle distance -- defined via an analogy, but why the shortest path curves on a globe is not fully intuitive.
Missed-sailing clause / expedited-alternate-carriage penalty -- understood as a contractual penalty, but not how the alternate carriage would practically happen.
Net revenue per TEU actually carried -- computable from given numbers, but the economic intuition for why this is the right comparison metric (vs. total profit) is not fully pictured.

MCS-51 (Q2): the draft-to-offload relationship as a uniform linear rate (0.15 cm/TEU) is vocabulary-comprehensible but not physically visualizable -- no diagram of the offload event or sense of scale is provided.
